## Definition

Let $A$ and $U$ be spaces of functions on bounded domains $D$ and $D'$. A family of finite-dimensional maps $(G_n)_{n\ge1}$ is a **discretization-invariant approximation** of an operator $G:A\to U$ if each $G_n$ accepts input samples from a discretization of $D$, returns values that can be queried at arbitrary points of $D'$, and approximates $G$ as the input discretization is refined. In the compact-uniform version, for every compact $K\subset A$,
$$\sup_{a\in K}\|G_n(a)-G(a)\|_U\longrightarrow0.$$
The statement is about a single continuum operator and its compatible discrete realizations. It does not declare unrelated grid-specific maps to be one operator family.
native_exact_changed_interfaces.actual_current_interface:
## Definition

Let $A$ and $U$ be real Banach spaces of functions on bounded domains $D$ and $D'$, with the input point evaluations used below defined. For every $n\ge1$, choose finite-dimensional normed spaces $E_n,F_n$, an exactly defined sampling map $S_n:A\to E_n$ (for example, $S_n(a)=(a(\xi_{n,1}),\ldots,a(\xi_{n,N_n}))$ at specified input points), a finite-dimensional map $\widetilde G_n:E_n\to F_n$, and an output reconstruction map $R_n:F_n\to U$. The reconstruction supplies a function with a defined value at every point of $D'$. The corresponding continuum-valued discrete map is
$$G_n(a):=R_n\bigl(\widetilde G_n(S_n(a))\bigr)\in U.$$
A family $(G_n)_{n\ge1}$ is a **discretization-invariant approximation** of an operator $G:A\to U$ if its sampling maps and output reconstructions are part of the family and it approximates this single continuum operator as the input discretization is refined. In the compact-uniform version, for every compact $K\subset A$,
$$\sup_{a\in K}\|G_n(a)-G(a)\|_U\longrightarrow0.$$
When $A$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes, the sampling map must be explicitly defined on those classes or use a specified representative convention; point evaluation is not inferred from the equivalence class alone. This definition does not identify unrelated grid-specific maps as one operator family.

native_exact_changed_interfaces.native_exact_before:
## Definition

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, let $\Gamma\subseteq\partial U$ be closed, let $L$ be a differential operator on $U$, and let $B$ be a boundary operator on $\Gamma$. Let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ and $g:\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ be target data. For a trial function $h$, define its residuals by $r_h(x)=L[h](x)-f(x)$ and $q_h(x)=B[h](x)-g(x)$. For $0<\alpha\le1$ and a function $v$ on a set $E$, define its Hölder seminorm by
$$[v]_{\alpha;E}=\sup_{x\ne y\in E}\frac{|v(x)-v(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For positive fixed weights $\lambda_r,\lambda_b$, and probability measures $\mu_r$ on $U$, $\mu_b$ on $\Gamma$, the population loss is
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)=\lambda_r\int_U|r_h|^2\,d\mu_r+\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|q_h|^2\,d\mu_b.$$
For residual collocation points $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}$ and boundary collocation points $x_b^1,\ldots,x_b^{m_b}$, the empirical loss is
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_{m}(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|r_h(x_r^i)|^2+\frac{\lambda_b}{m_b}\sum_{j=1}^{m_b}|q_h(x_b^j)|^2.$$
For $d\ge2$, its Hölder-regularized version is
$$\operatorname{Loss}_{m}(h;\lambda,\lambda_m^R)=\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^{2}+\lambda^R_{b,m}[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^{2}.$$
When $d=1$, all boundary points are available deterministically, no random boundary sample is used, and the source regularizes only the residual term. These are population and empirical functionals; they do not specify an optimization algorithm or assert that training reaches a global minimizer.
native_exact_changed_interfaces.actual_current_interface:
## Definition

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, let $\Gamma\subseteq\partial U$ be closed, let $L$ be a differential operator on $U$, and let $B$ be a boundary operator on $\Gamma$. Let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ and $g:\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ be target data. For a trial function $h$, define its residuals by $r_h(x)=L[h](x)-f(x)$ and $q_h(x)=B[h](x)-g(x)$. For $0<\alpha\le1$ and a function $v$ on a set $E$, define its Hölder seminorm by
$$[v]_{\alpha;E}=\sup_{x\ne y\in E}\frac{|v(x)-v(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
Only trial functions for which $L[h]$ on $U$ and $B[h]$ on $\Gamma$ are pointwise defined and finite are admitted. For the population loss, require $f,r_h$ to be measurable with respect to $(U,\mu_r)$ and $g,q_h$ to be measurable with respect to $(\Gamma,\mu_b)$. For positive fixed weights $\lambda_r,\lambda_b$ and probability measures $\mu_r$ on $U$, $\mu_b$ on $\Gamma$, the population loss is
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)=\lambda_r\int_U|r_h|^2\,d\mu_r+\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|q_h|^2\,d\mu_b.$$
These nonnegative population integrals take values in $[0,+\infty]$, so they may be infinite. The Hölder seminorms below may likewise be infinite.

For $d\ge2$, given positive integer counts $m_r,m_b$, residual collocation points $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}$, and boundary collocation points $x_b^1,\ldots,x_b^{m_b}$, the empirical loss is
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_{m}(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|r_h(x_r^i)|^2+\frac{\lambda_b}{m_b}\sum_{j=1}^{m_b}|q_h(x_b^j)|^2.$$
For $d=1$, a bounded Lipschitz domain has finite boundary, so $\Gamma$ is finite. When every point of $\Gamma$ is available deterministically, define its exact full-boundary contribution by
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b)=\lambda_b\sum_{y\in\Gamma}\mu_b(\{y\})|q_h(y)|^2=\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|q_h|^2\,d\mu_b,$$
and, for a positive integer count $m_r$ and residual collocation points $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}$, set
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_{m}(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|r_h(x_r^i)|^2+\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b).$$
For $d\ge2$, its Hölder-regularized version is
$$\operatorname{Loss}_{m}(h;\lambda,\lambda_m^R)=\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^{2}+\lambda^R_{b,m}[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^{2}.$$
For $d=1$, the Hölder-regularized version is
$$\operatorname{Loss}_{m}(h;\lambda,\lambda_m^R)=\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^{2};$$
it uses the exact full-boundary contribution above, has no random boundary sample, and has no boundary seminorm penalty. Require the regularization coefficients appearing in either version to be nonnegative; a zero coefficient contributes zero even when its seminorm is infinite. For finite realized sample lists the empirical sums are finite; the regularized objective is allowed to take the value $+\infty$. These are population and empirical functionals; they do not specify an optimization algorithm or assert that training reaches a global minimizer.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Each of the real spaces $L^p(D)$ for $1\le p<\infty$, $W^{m,p}(D)$ for $m\in\mathbb N$ and $1\le p<\infty$, and $C^m(\bar D)$ for $m\in\mathbb N_0$ has the approximation property: on every norm-compact subset, the identity can be approximated uniformly by bounded finite-rank linear maps. Here the $C^m$ norm is the maximum of the uniform norms of the derivatives through order $m$, extended continuously to $\bar D$. The same conclusion holds for the output-space list with its dimension and regularity parameters.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Each of the real spaces $L^p(D)$ for $1\le p<\infty$, $W^{m,p}(D)$ for $m\in\mathbb N$ and $1\le p<\infty$, and $C^m(\bar D)$ for $m\in\mathbb N_0$ has the approximation property: on every norm-compact subset, the identity can be approximated uniformly by bounded finite-rank linear maps. ## Definition

Choose $0<\alpha\le1$ and positive residual and boundary weights $\lambda_r,\lambda_b$. For $d\ge2$, let $\mu_r$ and $\mu_b$ be the residual and boundary sampling measures. The constants $c_r,c_b>0$ satisfy $\mu_r(U_j^\varepsilon)\ge c_r\varepsilon^d$ and $\mu_b(\Gamma_j^\varepsilon)\ge c_b\varepsilon^{d-1}$ for the cells in the sample partitions at the selected small scales $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_{0,r},\varepsilon_{0,b}$; $C_r,C_b>0$ satisfy $\mu_r(B_\varepsilon(x)\cap U)\le C_r\varepsilon^d$ and $\mu_b(B_\varepsilon(y)\cap\Gamma)\le C_b\varepsilon^{d-1}$. Require the upper ball-mass bounds at the selected fill radii, and take sample counts sufficiently large for both these radii and the partition scales to be in their specified ranges. Given sample counts $m_r,m_b$, put
$$\kappa_r=C_r/c_r,\qquad \kappa_b=C_b/c_b,$$
$$C_m=3\max\!\left\{\kappa_r(\sqrt d)^d m_r^{1/2},\ \kappa_b(\sqrt d)^{d-1}m_b^{1/2}\right\},$$
$$\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r(\sqrt d)^{2\alpha}c_r^{-2\alpha/d}m_r^{-\alpha/d}}{C_m},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{b,m}=\frac{3\lambda_b(\sqrt d)^{2\alpha}c_b^{-2\alpha/(d-1)}m_b^{-\alpha/(d-1)}}{C_m}.$$
Choose regularization weights componentwise at least these thresholds and satisfying $\|\lambda_m^R\|_\infty=O(\|\widehat\lambda_m^R\|_\infty)$ as sample counts grow. Evaluate the Hölder-regularized objective from the preceding definition on a trial class. For $d=1$, set
$$C_m=3\kappa_r m_r^{1/2},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{\lambda_r c_r^{-2\alpha}}{\kappa_r}m_r^{-\alpha-1/2},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{b,m}=0,$$
and use only the residual seminorm penalty. The thresholds are part of the source theorem and cannot be replaced by a generic positive penalty.
native_exact_changed_interfaces.actual_current_interface:
## Definition

Inputs are a dimension $d\ge1$, the data and operators specified in the physics-informed residual loss definition, $0<\alpha\le1$, positive weights $\lambda_r,\lambda_b$, and an admissible trial function $h$. The procedure returns the scalar empirical objective value $J_m(h)$. It uses the realized sample points and target values as inputs; it does not generate random samples.

For $d\ge2$, also supply positive integer counts $m_r,m_b$, residual samples $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}\in U$ with their observed values $f(x_r^i)$, boundary samples $x_b^1,\ldots,x_b^{m_b}\in\Gamma$ with their observed values $g(x_b^j)$, constants $c_r,c_b,C_r,C_b>0$, and small-scale cutoffs $\ell_{0,i},\rho_{0,i}>0$. At the selected partition scales $0<\ell_i\le\ell_{0,i}$, require cells $U_j^{\ell_r}$ and $\Gamma_j^{\ell_b}$ with masses at least $c_r\ell_r^d$ and $c_b\ell_b^{d-1}$, each contained in a cube of side $\ell_i$. Require upper ball-mass bounds $\mu_r(\overline B_\rho(x)\cap U)\le C_r\rho^d$ and $\mu_b(\overline B_\rho(y)\cap\Gamma)\le C_b\rho^{d-1}$ for every center and for all $0<\rho\le\rho_{0,i}$. The admissible counts satisfy, for $i\in\{r,b\}$,
$$m_i\ge\max\{1,c_i^{-2}\ell_{0,i}^{-2s_i},c_i^{-2}d^{s_i}\rho_{0,i}^{-2s_i}\},$$
so the computed partition scales and fill radii lie in the specified ranges.

For $d=1$, supply a positive integer $m_r$, residual samples $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}\in U$ with observed values $f(x_r^i)$, constants $c_r,C_r>0$, and cutoffs $\ell_{0,r},\rho_{0,r}>0$. At the residual scale $\ell_r$ below, require a finite measurable partition with each cell contained in an interval of length $\ell_r$ and mass at least $c_r\ell_r$, and require upper ball-mass bounds $\mu_r(\overline B_\rho(x)\cap U)\le C_r\rho$ for every center $x\in U$ and all $0<\rho\le\rho_{0,r}$. The admissible count satisfies
$$m_r\ge\max\{1,c_r^{-2}\ell_{0,r}^{-2},c_r^{-2}\rho_{0,r}^{-2}\},$$
so $\ell_r=\delta_r$ is in the specified ranges. Supply the observed boundary values at every point of the finite set $\Gamma$ with their masses $\mu_b(\{y\})$. No random boundary sample or boundary sample count is used.

For $d\ge2$, set $s_r=d$, $s_b=d-1$, and, for $i\in\{r,b\}$, compute
$$\ell_i=(c_i\sqrt{m_i})^{-1/s_i},\qquad \delta_i=\sqrt d\,\ell_i,\qquad \kappa_i=C_i/c_i,$$
$$C_m=3\max_{i\in\{r,b\}}\{\kappa_i d^{s_i/2}m_i^{1/2}\},\qquad
\widehat\lambda^R_{i,m}=\frac{3\lambda_i\delta_i^{2\alpha}}{C_m}.$$
For $d=1$, compute
$$\ell_r=\delta_r=(c_r\sqrt{m_r})^{-1},\qquad \kappa_r=C_r/c_r,\qquad C_m=3\kappa_r m_r^{1/2},$$
$$\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\delta_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m}
=\frac{\lambda_r c_r^{-2\alpha}}{\kappa_r}m_r^{-\alpha-1/2},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{b,m}=0.$$
For $d\ge2$, use supplied regularization weights $\lambda^R_{i,m}$ satisfying $\lambda^R_{i,m}\ge\widehat\lambda^R_{i,m}$ componentwise; for a sequence of sample counts also require $\|\lambda_m^R\|_\infty=O(\|\widehat\lambda_m^R\|_\infty)$. For $d=1$, set $\lambda^R_{b,m}=0$ and choose $\lambda^R_{r,m}\ge\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}$, with the corresponding one-coordinate max-norm order condition across a sequence of counts. If no residual weights are supplied, set them equal to their thresholds.

Finally evaluate and return $J_m(h)=\operatorname{Loss}_m(h;\lambda,\lambda_m^R)$ using the realized residual values, the realized boundary values when $d\ge2$, the exact weighted full-boundary contribution when $d=1$, and the residual seminorm penalty when $d=1$ or both seminorm penalties when $d\ge2$. The regularization thresholds are the source's exact thresholds and cannot be replaced by a generic positive penalty.

## Statement

Let $d\ge2$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^d$ be measurable, and let $\mu_r$ and $\mu_b$ be probability measures on them. For positive integers $m_r,m_b$, let the residual samples $x_1^r,\ldots,x_{m_r}^r$ and boundary samples $x_1^b,\ldots,x_{m_b}^b$ form $\varepsilon_r$- and $\varepsilon_b$-nets of $U$ and $\Gamma$ in Euclidean distance. Assume that for every center $x\in U$ and $y\in\Gamma$,
$$\mu_r(\overline B_{\varepsilon_r}(x)\cap U)\le C_r\varepsilon_r^d,\qquad \mu_b(\overline B_{\varepsilon_b}(y)\cap\Gamma)\le C_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}.$$
Suppose $[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}$, $[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}$, $[f]_{\alpha;U}$, and $[g]_{\alpha;\Gamma}$ are finite, where $[v]_{\alpha;E}=\sup_{x\ne y\in E}|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$. Let $\lambda_r,\lambda_b>0$, and use the population and empirical weighted-square PINN losses
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)=\lambda_r\int_U|L[h]-f|^2\,d\mu_r+\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|B[h]-g|^2\,d\mu_b,$$
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2+\frac{\lambda_b}{m_b}\sum_{j=1}^{m_b}|B[h](x_j^b)-g(x_j^b)|^2.$$
Define
$$C_m=3\max\{C_rm_r\varepsilon_r^d,\ C_bm_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}\},\quad \lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m},\quad \lambda^R_{b,m}=\frac{3\lambda_b\varepsilon_b^{2\alpha}}{C_m}.$$
Then
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)\le C_m\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+C_m\left(\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^2+\lambda^R_{b,m}[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^2\right)+3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;U}^2+3\lambda_b\varepsilon_b^{2\alpha}[g]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^2.$$

## Statement

For $d\ge2$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^d$ be measurable, and let $\mu_r$ and $\mu_b$ be probability measures on them. For positive integers $m_r,m_b$, let the residual samples $x_1^r,\ldots,x_{m_r}^r$ and boundary samples $x_1^b,\ldots,x_{m_b}^b$ form $\varepsilon_r$- and $\varepsilon_b$-nets of $U$ and $\Gamma$ in Euclidean distance. Assume that for every center $x\in U$ and $y\in\Gamma$,
$$\mu_r(\overline B_{\varepsilon_r}(x)\cap U)\le C_r\varepsilon_r^d,\qquad \mu_b(\overline B_{\varepsilon_b}(y)\cap\Gamma)\le C_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}.$$
Suppose $[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}$, $[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}$, $[f]_{\alpha;U}$, and $[g]_{\alpha;\Gamma}$ are finite, where $[v]_{\alpha;E}=\sup_{x\ne y\in E}|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$. Let $\lambda_r,\lambda_b>0$, and use the population and empirical weighted-square PINN losses
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)=\lambda_r\int_U|L[h]-f|^2\,d\mu_r+\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|B[h]-g|^2\,d\mu_b,$$
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2+\frac{\lambda_b}{m_b}\sum_{j=1}^{m_b}|B[h](x_j^b)-g(x_j^b)|^2.$$
Define
$$C_m=3\max\{C_rm_r\varepsilon_r^d,\ C_bm_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}\},\quad \lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m},\quad \lambda^R_{b,m}=\frac{3\lambda_b\varepsilon_b^{2\alpha}}{C_m}.$$
Then
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)\le C_m\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+C_m\left(\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^2+\lambda^R_{b,m}[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^2\right)+3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;U}^2+3\lambda_b\varepsilon_b^{2\alpha}[g]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^2.$$

For $d=1$, assume $\mu_r$ is a probability measure on measurable $U\subset\mathbb R$, and $\Gamma$ is a nonempty finite measurable set with probability measure $\mu_b$. Every point of $\Gamma$ is available deterministically. For a positive integer $m_r$, let $x_1^r,\ldots,x_{m_r}^r$ form an $\varepsilon_r$-net of $U$, and assume $\mu_r(\overline B_{\varepsilon_r}(x)\cap U)\le C_r\varepsilon_r$ for every center $x\in U$. Suppose the same four Hölder seminorms are finite. Use the exact weighted boundary loss
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b)=\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|B[h]-g|^2\,d\mu_b=\lambda_b\sum_{y\in\Gamma}\mu_b(\{y\})|B[h](y)-g(y)|^2$$
and the empirical loss $\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2+\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b)$. Set
$$C_m=3C_rm_r\varepsilon_r,\qquad \lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m},\qquad \lambda^R_{b,m}=0.$$
Then
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)\le C_m\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+C_m\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^2+3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;U}^2.$$
There is no random boundary term or boundary-data error term in this branch because the full boundary contribution is evaluated exactly.

example_domain_evidence.historical_example:
## Example

On $D=[0,1]$, define $G(a)(x)=\int_0^1a(y)\,dy$ for every $x\in[0,1]$. Its midpoint-mesh realization with $n$ cells is the constant output $G_n(a)(x)=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n a((j-\frac12)/n)$. For a fixed continuous input $a$, these outputs converge uniformly in $x$ to $G(a)$. By contrast, the identity map $F_n:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ on a length-$n$ vector is defined on a different input and output space at each $n$; without an additional reconstruction rule it is not a single function-space operator that accepts arbitrary meshes and can be queried at arbitrary output points.

For a fixed continuous input $a$, these outputs converge uniformly in $x$ to $G(a)$. By contrast, the identity map $F_n:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ on a length-$n$ vector is defined on a different input and output space at each $n$; without an additional reconstruction rule it is not a single function-space operator that accepts arbitrary meshes and can be queried at arbitrary output points.
